lessons.title: Start here: learning, scores and role boundaries
lessons.body:
# E07: PPE assessment, issue and care

This original VNDRLY course teaches decisions for common needs assessment; specialist ppe conditional. Its purpose is to make protection fit the exposure and worker. The six lessons explain the hazard, planning decisions, controls, checks, changing conditions and handback. Worked examples and two fictional scenarios show how those decisions fit together. Read the teaching before answering; no live hazardous activity is needed to complete this course.

There are six lesson knowledge checks and a 20-question final assessment. Submit each answer before viewing its feedback. Your first answer remains in the original score. If an answer is wrong, read the specific explanation and explicitly acknowledge the correction; acknowledged corrections contribute to a separate remediated score. Completion requires all sections and all 26 questions correct or explicitly acknowledged after remediation. A later corrected answer never erases the first-answer record.

Awareness means recognizing the hazard and knowing when to stop and seek help. Task competence means demonstrating assigned skills to a suitable assessor. Work authorization means the employer and site have approved a specific person, activity and conditions. These are separate decisions. Completing this course supports training evidence; it does not grant either of the latter two. Site instructions and applicable law control actual work; this course does not invent universal technical limits or approval intervals.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Assess the exposure before choosing equipment
lessons.body:
PPE protects a person against defined hazards within its performance limits. Selection starts with the task and exposure: impact, splash, heat, noise, airborne contaminants, electrical energy or other hazards. First consider eliminating or controlling the hazard through safer methods and engineering; PPE can remain essential but does not remove the source.

The assessment identifies the body areas exposed, severity, duration and conditions, then selects suitable protective performance. A standard site minimum is a baseline, not proof that every task-specific need is met. A brand or familiar color does not establish suitability.

Worked example: a worker handling a corrosive product receives ordinary work gloves because they are stocked. The competent assessment must establish chemical and task suitability; issue from a cabinet is not a hazard assessment.

### Applying the mechanism

Name the harm mechanism before selecting the item. A splash can reach skin or eyes, a flying particle can strike, heat can burn and airborne contaminants can be inhaled. Each mechanism calls for particular performance rather than the generic word “protection.” The assessment also considers whether the task can be changed to reduce exposure at the source. For example, a suitable closed transfer may reduce splash and vapor while PPE addresses the remaining risk. Workers must not redesign the process themselves, but they can report when the method forces repeated exposure. The competent owner then reviews both stronger controls and the protective equipment instead of treating PPE issue as the end of the assessment.

### Decision principles

Protective performance must match the harm mechanism. Brand familiarity cannot establish chemical, impact or thermal suitability.

A baseline addresses common conditions. Specialized work can introduce hazards beyond that baseline and needs its own assessment.

PPE has limitations and depends on correct selection and use. It does not remove stored energy, releases or the source of exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Match performance, compatibility and fit
lessons.body:
Different PPE classes protect against different hazards. Impact eyewear may not supply the needed splash protection; a face shield may need compatible eye protection beneath it. Gloves differ in chemical resistance, cut protection, heat performance and dexterity. The competent assessment and manufacturer information establish the correct combination.

Fit must allow the protective function while the worker performs the task. Combined equipment can interfere: eyewear, hearing protection, headgear and respirators may affect each other’s seal, position or field of view. Do not modify equipment informally to make an incompatible combination fit.

Worked example: new eyewear disrupts the seal of another protective device. The combination is reassessed and replaced or adjusted through the approved method before exposure, rather than accepting one protection at the expense of another.

### Applying the mechanism

Compatibility should be checked as the worker will actually use the equipment. Headgear, eyewear, hearing protection and respirators can compete for space or change a seal. Clothing and gloves can affect dexterity, snagging and access to controls. A protective combination that works while standing still may shift when reaching, kneeling or turning. The practical check should include those relevant movements in a safe setting. If the worker cannot perform the task while preserving coverage and fit, reassess the combination or work method. Removing one required item or cutting a strap informally can defeat protection. A suitable alternative must preserve the relevant functions together.

### Decision principles

Different glove materials and constructions protect against different exposures. Thickness and marketing terms cannot establish the required performance.

The protective function must persist in use. Static comfort alone does not prove that coverage or compatibility remains adequate during work.

Unapproved modification can alter protection and fit. The responsible program should provide a suitable alternative rather than requiring an improvised compromise.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Issue equipment and teach correct use
lessons.body:
Issue the correct type and size with understandable instruction. Training covers when protection is needed, how to put it on and remove it, adjustment, limitations, inspection, cleaning, storage and replacement. The worker demonstrates the required use; a receipt establishes delivery, not competence.

Some equipment requires additional program prerequisites. Respirators can require medical evaluation, fit testing and specific training under the applicable respiratory program. Electrical, fall-protection and specialist PPE also have task-specific assessment needs. This course does not replace those programs.

Worked example: a worker signs for a respirator but has not completed the required respiratory prerequisites. The signature does not authorize exposure; the respiratory program must establish readiness separately.

### Applying the mechanism

Instruction should explain limitations with concrete examples. A chemical glove can protect against an assessed substance without resisting every solvent; impact eyewear may not provide the same coverage as a splash arrangement; a filtering facepiece does not supply oxygen. The worker needs to know what not to assume when the task changes. Demonstration then establishes fitting, adjustment, inspection, use and removal for the assigned item. A trainer should correct specific errors and observe the corrected action rather than merely repeat the explanation. Where a specialist program requires medical, fit or technical prerequisites, keep them as separate recorded decisions. A general PPE receipt or quiz must never be relabeled as those results.

### Decision principles

Workers need to know how the item protects and when it no longer does. A slogan cannot guide safe inspection or replacement.

Respiratory protection has specialized selection and user prerequisites. General awareness and ownership do not establish those conditions.

Demonstration can reveal fitting and use errors that attendance records miss. Language and delivery must allow the worker to understand the actual instruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Inspect before use and recognize loss of protection
lessons.body:
Check PPE using the relevant manufacturer and program criteria. Look for damage, contamination, wear, missing parts, degraded materials and status or expiry requirements where applicable. Do not use damaged protection because the task will be short. Some failures are not obvious, so follow event-based and service-life rules as well as visual checks.

The inspection must fit the item. A scratch on eyewear, cut glove, cracked shell or damaged connector can have different disposition criteria. When the user cannot establish acceptance, hold exposure and obtain the competent responsible decision.

Worked example: chemical gloves appear intact after contact but their safe use period or contamination status is uncertain. The worker follows the chemical-specific program rather than assuming no visible hole means continued protection.

### Applying the mechanism

Inspection criteria can include condition that is not obvious from a quick look. Chemical contact, heat, age, an impact or another abnormal event may require replacement or specialist disposition even if the item remains intact. Follow the applicable manufacturer and program requirements rather than waiting for a visible hole or crack. Users should understand any event that requires immediate removal from reliance and how to obtain a suitable replacement. If identifying information or required status is missing, the owner resolves it through the approved process. Do not guess a protection class from color or assume that more layers make an unknown item suitable for a different hazard.

### Decision principles

Different protection fails in different ways. Criteria must match the material, design and hazard rather than a generic appearance check.

Hazard consequences do not depend on the worker’s intended duration. A brief event can occur immediately, so required protection must be effective at the start.

Uncertainty must remain visible. The user should not create a technical acceptance decision they are not qualified to make.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Clean, store and replace without transferring exposure
lessons.body:
Care preserves protection and prevents contamination reaching the worker, other people or clean areas. Follow the manufacturer and hazard-specific cleaning method; an unsuitable cleaner can damage materials. Store equipment away from the conditions that degrade it and separate contaminated or rejected items from ready stock.

Doffing can expose skin or clothing to contamination. Use the taught method and disposal or decontamination arrangements for the actual hazard. Do not take contaminated equipment home casually or share items without the required hygiene and fit controls.

Worked example: a worker removes contaminated gloves and touches their face with the outer surface. Practical instruction corrects the removal sequence and provides the required hygiene arrangements before further work.

### Applying the mechanism

Care begins when the worker leaves the exposure area. Contaminated outer surfaces can transfer material during removal, transport or storage. The task-specific method establishes where doffing occurs, how contaminated items are contained and whether they are cleaned, decontaminated or disposed of. A worker should not take potentially contaminated gear home for ordinary laundry without an approved arrangement. Cleaning products and drying conditions can also damage protective materials, so use the specified method. Ready equipment needs protected storage separate from rejected or contaminated items. If shared equipment is allowed, the program addresses hygiene, fitting and condition for the next user rather than assuming that wiping the surface restores every requirement.

### Decision principles

Cleaning can degrade materials or spread contamination. The method must suit the equipment and substance.

Protection can be defeated during handling after the task. Practical removal and hygiene steps must match the actual contamination.

Ordering equipment does not protect a worker now. Work must remain controlled until a suitable effective item and its prerequisites are available.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reassess problems and preserve qualification boundaries
lessons.body:
Reassess when tasks, products, equipment, environment or worker needs change, and when discomfort or interference prevents correct use. Do not treat a reported problem as refusal without examining whether the selected equipment fits and protects. Involve the worker and competent program owner in finding a suitable arrangement.

Records should link the hazard assessment, selected equipment, issue, training and observed use, while protecting any medical information in the proper program. Review whether PPE is worn correctly and whether stronger controls could reduce reliance. A general written pass is not a respirator fit test, electrical qualification or fall-protection demonstration.

Worked example: several workers remove eye protection because it fogs and obscures the task. The owner addresses compatibility and conditions rather than merely collecting new signatures.

### Applying the mechanism

A reported fit or usability problem is information about control performance. Fogging, slipping, restricted movement or conflicting equipment can cause workers to use protection incorrectly or create another hazard. The supervisor should establish a safe interim arrangement and obtain competent review, involving the worker in checking the proposed solution. Observation after the change asks whether the item now protects during the actual task, not just whether a replacement was issued. The program should also examine whether stronger controls can reduce dependence on PPE. Practical qualification remains specific: demonstrating gloves and eyewear does not qualify a person for respiratory equipment, fall arrest or energized electrical work.

### Decision principles

Selection is bounded by assumptions. Changed exposure or fit can invalidate the prior assessment before any incident occurs.

Delivery and attendance do not establish effective use. Observation checks whether the selected protection works in the actual task.

Specialist protective systems have their own prerequisites and practical evaluations. A written general PPE course cannot substitute for them.

lessons.title: Two applied scenarios and worked decisions
lessons.body:
## Applied scenarios: complete worked decisions

### Scenario 1: A new cleaning product

A shop changes cleaning chemical but keeps issuing the same gloves. The worker notices softening and is told all gloves are chemical gloves.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** Affected handling is held while the competent assessment uses the actual product and manufacturer information to select suitable protection and stronger controls where appropriate. Damaged or contaminated gloves are controlled and replaced. Workers receive instruction in the new limitations, inspection, removal and care. The old issue record does not establish compatibility with the new chemical.

### Scenario 2: The signed respirator receipt

A worker has signed for a tight-fitting respirator and passed this PPE course. The required respiratory program prerequisites and fit evaluation have not been established.

**Worked decision and reasoning.** The worker is not assigned exposure requiring that respirator. The respiratory program establishes the appropriate hazard assessment, selection, medical and fit prerequisites where required, training and practical use. The general course and issue receipt remain learning and delivery evidence only. They are not relabeled as a medical clearance or fit-test result.

lessons.title: Final assessment: 20 individual decisions
lessons.body: Answer the 20 questions individually using the taught principles. Each submission preserves your first answer. Review feedback after submitting. When an answer is incorrect, explicitly acknowledge the correct decision and explanation before moving on. The result must show both the first-answer score and the remediated score across all 26 questions. Do not attempt a live hazardous task to obtain an answer; the assessment is a knowledge and judgment exercise.

lessons.title: Completion and separately assessed practical competence
lessons.body:
## What this completion means

The course is complete only after every section and all 26 questions have been accomplished, through correct responses or explicit acknowledgment of the supplied correction. Preserve the original and remediated results separately. Acknowledgment is a learning action, not evidence that the learner has performed the task safely in the field.

## Separate practical evaluation

A competent assessor must observe correct selection understanding, fitting, adjustment, combined-equipment compatibility, inspection, use, removal, care and replacement for the assigned PPE. Respiratory, electrical, hearing, fall-protection and other specialist programs retain their own technical and practical requirements. This course does not grant hazardous-task authorization or replace a fit test.

An assessor must record the actual role, equipment or task, procedure used, conditions demonstrated, observed performance, limitations, corrective coaching and final decision. Use safe simulation where exposing a learner would create danger. A provider certificate, company evidence score and site permit answer different questions; none should be substituted for the others. The employer and operating/site authority retain the final task and site readiness decisions. A failed or unassessed critical practical step remains a restriction even after a perfect written score.

questions.prompt: Ordinary work gloves are offered for an unassessed corrosive product. What is required?

options.label: Hazard-based selection using the actual product and task information.
Use them because gloves are mandatory.
Double any glove and assume protection.

questions.prompt: What should PPE selection start with?

options.label: The preferred supplier logo.
The most common site color.
The actual hazard, exposure and task conditions.

questions.prompt: Does site-minimum PPE clear every task?

options.label: Yes, if everyone wears the same set.
No; task-specific assessment can require different or additional protection.
Yes, minimum means complete.

questions.prompt: What is PPE’s place in the control system?

options.label: Protection for assessed exposure alongside stronger controls where appropriate.
Automatic replacement for isolation or engineering controls.
Proof the hazard has disappeared.

questions.prompt: Two required protective items interfere with each other’s fit. What happens?

options.label: Remove whichever item is uncomfortable.
Modify the equipment without approval.
Reassess and establish a compatible effective combination before exposure.

questions.prompt: What establishes glove suitability?

options.label: Only the word “industrial.”
The actual hazard and manufacturer performance information for the use conditions.
Only thickness.

questions.prompt: Why assess PPE fit during the actual task?

options.label: Movement and combined equipment can change coverage, seal and usability.
Fit matters only while standing still.
One size fits every worker safely.

questions.prompt: Can a worker casually modify PPE for comfort?

options.label: Yes, cutting straps is always acceptable.
Yes, if the item still looks similar.
No; only approved adjustments or alternatives preserve verified performance.

questions.prompt: A worker signed a PPE issue receipt. What does that establish?

options.label: Completion of all respiratory prerequisites.
Delivery or acknowledgment of issue, not demonstrated correct use.
Competence for every hazardous task.

questions.prompt: What should PPE instruction include?

options.label: Use, adjustment, limitations, inspection, care and replacement.
Only the item’s price.
Only a reminder to wear it.

questions.prompt: What can respirator use require beyond issue?

options.label: Only a spare filter.
Only this general PPE quiz.
Applicable medical evaluation, fit testing and program-specific training.

questions.prompt: How should comprehension be checked?

options.label: Only asking whether the worker has questions.
Observed demonstration and explanation in an understandable form.
Only counting signatures.

questions.prompt: A chemical glove looks intact but its acceptable continued use is uncertain. What is required?

options.label: Follow the product- and program-specific disposition before further exposure.
Keep using it until a hole appears.
Wash it with any solvent.

questions.prompt: What should a pre-use PPE check follow?

options.label: One visual rule for every protective item.
Only whether the item is clean.
The actual item’s manufacturer and program criteria.

questions.prompt: Does a short task justify damaged PPE?

options.label: Yes, if the worker is experienced.
No; suitable protection is required before exposure.
Yes, if under a minute.

questions.prompt: What if acceptance is beyond the user’s competence?

options.label: Hold exposure and obtain competent disposition or suitable replacement.
Guess a pass.
Ask an unrelated coworker to sign.

questions.prompt: Contaminated PPE is placed with clean ready stock. What must happen?

options.label: Use it first so the stock clears.
Assume drying makes it clean.
Control contamination and restore the approved segregation and care arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which cleaning method should be used?

options.label: Only whichever method is fastest.
The manufacturer and hazard-specific approved method.
Any strong solvent available.

questions.prompt: Why teach removal as well as wearing?

options.label: Doffing can transfer contamination to skin, clothing or clean areas.
Once work ends the hazard disappears.
Removal cannot affect exposure.

questions.prompt: What should replacement arrangements ensure?

options.label: Workers use damaged items until the next order.
Only a purchase request is submitted.
Suitable protection is available before exposed work resumes.

questions.prompt: Workers report fogging that prevents safe vision. What is the useful response?

options.label: Tell workers to remove protection whenever needed.
Reassess the equipment and conditions and establish a suitable effective solution.
Ignore it because PPE was issued.

questions.prompt: What changes should trigger PPE reassessment?

options.label: Task, product, exposure, equipment combination or user needs.
Only the annual purchase cycle.
Only a serious injury.

questions.prompt: What should PPE assurance compare?

options.label: Only quantities purchased.
Only signature totals.
The assessment and issue records with actual correct use and protective condition.

questions.prompt: What qualification does this general course not provide?

options.label: Knowledge of inspection limits.
Respirator fit testing, electrical task qualification or fall-protection practical competence.
Awareness of reporting duties.

questions.prompt: What assumption failed in the cleaning scenario?

options.label: That a prior glove selection applies to every chemical and use condition.
That workers should inspect gloves.
That issue records can be retained.

questions.prompt: What must remain separate from the receipt and written score?

options.label: Only the equipment color.
Only the supplier’s invoice.
The respiratory program’s required selection, clearance, fit and practical-use decisions.
